appraisal_events.evidence: « Mes parents malheureusement s'en remirent à des principes entièrement différents de ceux que je leur suggérais d'adopter, quand ils voulurent apprécier l'action de mon oncle. Mon père et mon grand-père eurent avec lui des explications violentes » ; « il est mort bien des années après sans qu'aucun de nous l'ait jamais revu ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Once the child reports the visit, the family judges the uncle's action by their own standards, confronts him violently, and cuts him off permanently. The narrator reports this family condemnation without endorsing it — the word « malheureusement » and his own gratitude mark his distance — but the practical outcome is the uncle's total expulsion from the family circle.

appraisal_events.evidence: « la nouvelle importance dont j'étais doué » ; « Je m'imaginais, comme tout le monde, que le cerveau des autres était un réceptacle inerte et docile » ; « Je résolus de m'abstenir de ce geste insuffisant et je détournai la tête. Mon oncle pensa que je suivais en cela les ordres de mes parents ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The retrospective narrator stages his younger self's vanity and misjudgment as a self-indictment: his boast destroys the very benefactor he wanted to thank, and his excess of feeling produces a gesture read as a snub, leaving him with irreparable remorse.

status_effects.explanation: He is definitively excluded from the family: violent scenes with father and grandfather, then a rupture that lasts until his death without anyone seeing him again.

The family treats his conduct as a fault worth violent reproach; the passage's small touches (the lie about the boy's prizes, the silent refusal to lend his books) reinforce a locally lowered appraisal, even though the narrator himself keeps calling him kind.
His adoration and gratitude turn into « la douleur, la reconnaissance, le remords » that he can never express; the loss is presented as permanent and his own doing.

ambiguities: The visitor is only ever « la dame en rose » in this passage; the identification with Odette comes from the reference sheet and later text, not from the local wording.

The narrator's stance toward the parents' condemnation is layered: « malheureusement » and his own tenderness for the uncle withhold endorsement, yet he also concedes he caused real harm, so the family's blame is reported as consequential without being clearly ratified.
